page-gather-fresh-grass: Cut tall grass with a knife or scythe. It leaves a fresh ground layer; Sneak while harvesting to collect fresh grass. Collect ten artofgrowing:grass. Keep it separate from dry hay and cereal straw. This obtain goal checks the collected material, not the cutting gesture.
check-dry-grass: I have dried fresh grass into hay.
page-dry-grass: Leave fresh grass as a ground layer in suitable warm weather, or place collected fresh grass in a sheltered ground pile with Sneak + right-click. Wait until it becomes game:drygrass. Rain can reset field drying and cold stops it; a fixed elapsed-time promise is not reliable. Tick only after you have seen the grass become hay. The next quest checks ten collected hay.
check-convert-hay-straw-blocks: I have converted a hay or straw pile into blocks.
page-convert-hay-straw-blocks: Place hay or cereal straw in its Art of Growing ground pile and add enough for the pile’s block-conversion action. With hay, use Ctrl + Sneak + right-click to make the pile rather than starting a firepit. Use Ctrl + Sneak + right-click on the pile when block conversion is offered, then collect the block. This is the replacement for the disabled ordinary haybale grid recipe. Hay and straw produce their own blocks; the Art of Growing thatch-bed recipe needs three artofgrowing:thatchhay-normal-ud straw blocks. Tick after actually converting a pile, not just owning loose grass.
check-harvest-cereal-bundles: I have harvested a ripe cereal crop into wet bundles.
page-harvest-cereal-bundles: Plant cereal seeds on farmland and harvest ripe rye, spelt, rice or amaranth. Art of Growing leaves wet bundles rather than ready grain. Knife or scythe harvesting can create a ground pile. Tick after harvesting a ripe cereal crop into wet bundles; do not tick merely for finding or buying grain.
page-dry-cereal-bundles: Place wet cereal bundles with Sneak + right-click on ground sheltered from rain and out of water. Let them become dry bundles. There is no mandatory drying rack. Pick up four dry bundles to register this goal, then put them back in a ground pile for threshing. Do not leave wet bundles in inventory indefinitely; they can spoil into straw.
check-thresh-cereal-bundles: I have threshed a dry cereal pile with a stick or flail.
page-thresh-cereal-bundles: Hold right-click on a dry cereal ground pile with a stick. Threshing releases planting seeds and straw (game:thatch); a flail is a later speed upgrade, not a starting requirement. Tick after actually threshing a dry cereal pile. Do not use the soybean held-shelling interaction on cereal bundles.
page-hull-cereal-seeds: Collect threshed seeds and reserve some for planting and suitable trough feed. In the crafting grid, combine spare seeds with a knife tool: one supported seed gives one culinary grain. Collect four grain. The preserved harvest goal follows with a larger food supply; grain is not the same item as a planting seed bag.
page-harvest-flax-bundles: Plant flax and harvest the ripe crop into artofgrowing:grainbundle-flax-wet. Collect sixteen wet bundles to register this goal. If cutting leaves them in a ground pile, collect them before replacing them for drying. The crop does not directly yield usable fibers.
page-dry-flax-bundles: Place the wet flax cereal bundles in sheltered ground storage out of water and wait for the dry bundle state. Collect sixteen dry cereal bundles, then replace them on the ground for stick threshing. These grainbundle-flax-dry bundles are not yet the dry flax stalks used for retting.
page-thresh-flax-stalks: Hold right-click on the dry flax cereal pile with a stick. This releases flax seeds and artofgrowing:flaxbundle-dry stalks instead of the ordinary cereal straw. Keep planting seeds and collect sixteen dry stalks. A flail is optional; do not knife-hull the stalks.
page-ret-flax-stalks: Put the dry flax stalks into an Art of Growing ground pile occupying a water block. Let them ret until they become soaked flax, artofgrowing:flaxbundle-wet, then collect sixteen. Rain alone is not the water-block condition. This is not a sealed-barrel fermentation recipe and drying the soaked stalks is not the next step.
page-wash-flax-stalks: Wash soaked flax with water to make artofgrowing:flaxbundle-clear. The barrel recipe uses a litre of water without a timed sealed fermentation; the grid also offers a water-filled bucket, fired bowl or fired jug route. Check the displayed liquid-container recipe. Collect sixteen clean stalks; do not wait for a nonexistent clean-to-dry transition.
page-soften-flax-stalks: Hold clean flax in your main hand and hold right-click without Sneak for about two seconds. This makes soft/crumpled flax, artofgrowing:flaxbundle-soft. Collect sixteen. A creaser in the offhand speeds batches, and floor sitting can enlarge them, but bare-hand softening works for your first fibers.
page-make-flax-ridge: Make a rough ridge from three sticks and a rope, using the reed or vine rope route so you do not need fibers or twine first. An available wooden ridge is another route. Put the ridge in your offhand and soft flax in your main hand, then hold right-click without Sneak to comb fibers. The ridge is required and wears with use; the creaser and flail are optional upgrades.
check-prepare-winter-feed: I have stored and checked suitable winter livestock feed.
page-prepare-winter-feed: Before winter, dry grass into hay while the weather allows it, collect cereal straw, and set aside the named seed or other feed accepted by your animals’ troughs. Store the reserve dry, inspect aging, and confirm a sample is accepted by the intended trough for those animals. Aged grass is not an added Art of Growing feed. Tick only after checking the reserve and actual feed acceptance. Owning perishable hay alone is not proof of winter readiness.
page-bricklayers-bricklayers-clay-and-fi:
Four raw daub make two mudbricks in the crafting grid. Mudbricks need no firing.

The existing raw-daub recipes use dried hay (game:drygrass), while Art of Growing adds alternatives using cereal straw (game:thatch). Check the handbook for the chosen soil, sand and clay recipe. Thresh dried cereal bundles for straw; fresh grass, dried hay and straw are different materials.
page-efchefstricks-efchefstricks-baking-:
Bread crumbs alone in the crafting grid make bread crumb feed. You can't eat it, but many animals will, and it's a cheap way to keep livestock fed.

Prepare culinary grain from threshed seed bags with a knife before baking the bread used here. Crumb feed is a Chef’s Tricks recipe; do not assume any seed bag is an equivalent bait or feed.
page-expandedfoods-expandedfoods-baking-:
Put grain in a hot clay oven and take it out once it's roasted. Roasted grain goes into porridge and pilaf, and keeps longer than raw grain.

Use hulled culinary grain, not wet bundles or planting seed bags. Dry cereal bundles in sheltered ground piles, thresh the dry pile with a stick, and keep seed bags for planting. Use a knife with spare seeds in the crafting grid to make culinary grain.
page-expandedfoods-expandedfoods-farming:
Fill the fruit press with flax grain, sunflower seeds or soybeans and press it. Cooking oil fries breaded food and enriches dough.

Shell soybean bundles into beans; use the culinary grain or sunflower seeds requested by the oil recipe, not whole harvested bundles. Reserve planting stock before processing food.

Harvest ripe soybeans as Art of Growing soybean bundles. Hold a bundle and right-click without Sneak to shell it into soybeans; collect eight beans. The beans themselves can be planted, so reserve some before making oil, milk or sauce. Soybean bundles use held shelling, not the cereal drying-and-stick-threshing chain.

Seal soybeans in a barrel with a litre of water for each. Three days later they're soaked, ready to become soy sauce or soy milk.

First hold right-click with harvested soybean bundles to shell them into beans. This food soak is separate from the water retting used for flax.

Mix the soybean powder with a grain, such as spelt, rice or flax, in the crafting grid or the mixing bowl.

Use shelled soybeans for the soybean preparation and hulled culinary grain for the grain ingredient. Raw bundles and planting bags are not interchangeable with those food inputs.

Seal cultured soybeans with a litre of brine each for a week, then press the slurry in the fruit press. A litre of soy sauce takes about seven cultured beans. Start with beans shelled from soybean bundles; reserve plantable soybeans before processing your food stock.
page-expandedfoods-expandedfoods-kitchen:
Put raw meat in a lit firepit and take it out once it's cooked. Cooked meat fills you up and won't make you sick.

For the Art of Growing firepit, start with dried hay, not freshly cut grass, then finish and light the firepit before cooking. Keep the saucepan and cooked-meat goals shown below; Art of Growing does not replace those food outputs.

Craft a mixing bowl with a table and a wooden axle into a powered mixing bowl, and connect a turning axle to its bottom. It kneads on its own, and puts what it makes beside it, or into a hopper.

For grain-based mixtures, prepare culinary grain by knife-hulling spare threshed seeds first. The powered bowl remains a kitchen upgrade, not a substitute for crop processing.
page-expandedfoods-expandedfoods-stone-a:
Break a cut cattail again to dig up its root, faster with a shovel. Roast the root on a lit firepit: it's plain, but it keeps you going when nothing else will.

For the Art of Growing firepit, start with dried hay, not freshly cut grass, then finish and light the firepit before cooking. Keep the Expanded Foods charred-root outcome shown below.
page-vanilla-arms-and-armor-make-crude-s: Six sticks and three cattail tops, papyrus tops or bamboo stakes make a crude shield. Hold it in your offhand and Sneak to block. See the armor guide. Use the cattail or papyrus material named by the recipe. Reeds, fresh grass, hay and straw are different materials; do not substitute straw for reeds.
page-vanilla-arms-and-armor-make-improvi: Art of Growing adds a straw route to improvised wooden body armor: use firewood, straw (game:thatch) and a knife tool in the crafting grid. This added recipe does not require rope; other available recipes may use different materials. The armor breaks quickly, but can save your life.
page-vanilla-baking-grind-flour:
Put grain in the quern and turn it.

Dry cereal bundles in sheltered ground piles, thresh the dry pile with a stick, and keep seed bags for planting. Use a knife with spare seeds in the crafting grid to make culinary grain. Put the resulting grain, not the bundle or seed bag, into the quern.
page-vanilla-baking-eat-well:
Your character panel shows five food groups: fruit, vegetables, grain, protein and dairy. Keeping all of them full raises your maximum health, so keep a varied larder.

For bread, first dry and thresh cereal bundles, hull spare seeds with a knife, then grind the grain. Harvest vegetables at their food stage while leaving separate plants for seed.
page-vanilla-beekeeping-raid-wild-hive:
Wild bee hives hang in trees and hide in hollow logs. Breaking one gives honeycomb, but angers the bees and ends that colony. Leave one standing if you want to catch a swarm.

Use the cattail or papyrus material named by the recipe. Reeds, fresh grass, hay and straw are different materials; do not substitute straw for reeds.
page-vanilla-beekeeping-make-skep:
A skep is woven from cattail or papyrus tops and sealed with clay, in the crafting grid. It's a home for bees.

Use the cattail or papyrus material named by the recipe. Reeds, fresh grass, hay and straw are different materials; do not substitute straw for reeds.
page-vanilla-beekeeping-squeeze-honey:
Hold honeycomb over an open container, such as a bowl or bucket, and squeeze it to get honey and beeswax. A fruit press does it faster. Each comb gives a fifth of a litre.

Keep reeds for reed recipes and beeswax for its own recipes. Art of Growing does not turn cattail tops into straw.
page-vanilla-beekeeping-make-candle:
Cook three beeswax and one flax fiber in a pot over the fire to make a candle.

Flax fibers come after drying and threshing flax bundles, retting the stalks in water, washing, softening and offhand-ridge combing; the crop itself does not give ready fibers. Save fully combed fibers for the candle wick.
page-vanilla-building-make-roof: Make eight roofing pieces. Art of Growing adds straw roofing in its own material family; ordinary game roofing also counts. Thresh dried cereal bundles for straw, then check the roof recipe for its other inputs. Fresh grass, hay and straw are not interchangeable, and roofs protect drying piles from rain.
page-vanilla-clay-and-fire-form-bowl:
Hold clay, then shift and right-click the ground to start clay forming. Pick the bowl, and add clay with right-click and remove it with left-click, layer by layer.

Dry hay or straw can start the first pit-kiln layer; freshly cut grass cannot. If you use hay, let the cut grass dry before loading the kiln.
page-vanilla-clay-and-fire-fire-pottery: Place raw pottery on the ground with Sneak + right-click and build a pit kiln. For the first layer, use dried hay or the added straw alternative, then load the usual sticks and firewood and light it. Fresh grass is not kiln tinder. Wait for the kiln to finish and collect fired pottery.
page-vanilla-clay-and-fire-make-bricks:
Four clay make a raw brick in the crafting grid. Fire the raw bricks in a pit kiln. Fired bricks, set in mortar, build walls that last.

The pit kiln accepts dried hay or the added straw alternative for its first layer, then the usual sticks and firewood. Do not load fresh grass or aged grass as a guessed substitute.
page-vanilla-clay-and-fire-cook-meal:
Put the pot in a lit firepit with ingredients inside it, wait for it to cook, and take it out. A mixed meal fills you up far better than its parts.

For the Art of Growing firepit, start with dried hay, not freshly cut grass, then finish and light the firepit before cooking. Use the existing cooking-pot recipe and collect the cooked pot.
page-vanilla-copper-age-make-charcoal: Dig a pit, fill it with full stacks of firewood and cover it with blocks that don't burn, leaving the top of one stack open. Build a firepit on that stack, light it, and seal it within half an hour. See the charcoal burning guide. Build the starting firepit with dried hay rather than fresh grass; keep the charcoal pit sealed as the guide describes.
page-vanilla-copper-age-make-scythe: Smith a scythe head and fit it to a stick. It cuts a wider area, but Art of Growing grass starts as fresh ground layers and cereal crops become wet bundles. Dry grass into hay; dry cereal bundles and thresh them with a stick before hulling spare seeds into grain. The scythe does not bypass those steps.
page-vanilla-farming-gather-seeds: Collect four planting seeds. Ripe cereal crops give wet bundles: dry them in sheltered ground piles, then hold right-click on the dry pile with a stick to release seeds. Vegetable crops have separate food and later seed stages; reserve seed-bearing plants. Do not turn all planting seeds into food grain.
page-vanilla-farming-harvest-grain: Bring in sixteen culinary grain. Harvest ripe rye, spelt, rice or amaranth as wet bundles, place them with Sneak + right-click and dry them under shelter. Hold right-click on the dry ground pile with a stick to thresh seeds and straw. Reserve seeds for planting; craft spare seeds with a knife into grain. Collect the grain in your inventory to register this goal.
page-vanilla-farming-grow-vegetables: Harvest twelve edible vegetables, not the final seed-and-rot stage. Carrot and onion peak at stage 7, turnip at 5, parsnip at 8 and cabbage at 12. Leave some plants to reach their later seed stage. Carrot, onion, turnip and parsnip vegetables can also be replanted for a separate seed crop; do not assume cabbage has that same route.
page-vanilla-farming-make-quern:
A quern grinds grain into flour. Two sticks and four full blocks of granite, andesite, basalt or peridotite make one, with a hammer and chisel in the crafting grid. A rock block comes out whole once everything around it has been dug away.

Dry cereal bundles in sheltered ground piles, thresh the dry pile with a stick, and keep seed bags for planting. Use a knife with spare seeds in the crafting grid to make culinary grain. The quern processes the resulting grain; it does not thresh bundles.
page-vanilla-farming-grow-pumpkin: Grow pumpkins on farmland with room for vines and fruit. Collect a ripe pumpkin fruit to register the first goal. Place a ripe fruit and hold right-click on it with a knife or cleaver to cut it into edible pumpkin and seeds; collect the pumpkin pieces for the second goal. Reserve planting seeds before using the separate knife-hulling recipe for culinary pumpkin grain. Pumpkin cutting is not the cereal bundle drying-and-threshing process.
page-vanilla-farming-full-harvest: Gather the grain and vegetables shown below after establishing your flax supply. Grain is the hulled food output after drying bundles and threshing; vegetables are harvested at their food stage. Keep planting seeds and seed-bearing plants aside. Fully processed flax fibers, not freshly cut stalks, finish the textile branch.
page-vanilla-husbandry-make-trough: Place a small trough for chickens. Art of Growing adds named cereal seed bags and pumpkin grain to its feeds alongside existing options. Check that the offered feed is accepted for chickens; not every bundle or grass material is suitable. Owning a trough does not prove that animals have been fed.
page-vanilla-husbandry-make-large-trough: Place a large trough and offer feed suited to the animals in the pen. Art of Growing adds fresh grass, straw, straw blocks, named seed bags and some legume bundles alongside existing feeds. These materials are not nutritionally interchangeable, and aged grass is not an added feed. Confirm that the trough accepts the chosen feed for your animals.
page-vanilla-husbandry-breed-animals: Keep a male and female of the same kind in a secure pen and provide a species-appropriate accepted feed. Grain remains one option; Art of Growing adds particular seed, grass and straw feeds to particular troughs. Prepare dry feed before winter and inspect it for aging. Tick this quest only after the first young are actually born, not after filling a trough.
page-vanilla-husbandry-make-henbox: Make and place a henbox. Art of Growing adds a nest recipe using straw (game:thatch) with planks; check the available recipe rather than substituting fresh grass. Hens need suitable feed, a rooster nearby and eggs to brood. A placed box alone does not prove hatching.
page-vanilla-husbandry-make-basket-trap:
A basket of cattail or papyrus tops and a stick make a basket trap. Bait it with food the animal likes and it may catch chickens, hares and many young animals.

Use the cattail or papyrus material named by the recipe. Reeds, fresh grass, hay and straw are different materials; do not substitute straw for reeds. Choose a bait accepted by this trap and animal; trough seed support does not establish trap-bait support.
page-vanilla-husbandry-make-crate-trap:
A reinforced crate trap is built from planks and bronze or better nails and strips. It catches larger animals than a basket trap, but tiny baits like grain won't do.

Use bait accepted by the crate trap and intended animal. Art of Growing’s added trough feeds do not make every seed bag or bundle valid trap bait.
page-vanilla-husbandry-melt-fat:
Pigs, sheep, goats, deer, bears and raccoons leave raw fat when you harvest them. Cook it in a pot over the fire and it sets into lumps of rendered fat, used for pelts, the fruit press and sealing crocks.

For the Art of Growing firepit, start with dried hay, not freshly cut grass, then finish and light the firepit before cooking. The rendered-fat outcome is unchanged.
page-vanilla-kitchen-roast-meat:
Put raw meat in a lit firepit and take it out once it's cooked. Cooked meat fills you up and won't make you sick.

For the Art of Growing firepit, start with dried hay, not freshly cut grass, then finish and light the firepit before cooking. Collect the cooked poultry specified below.
page-vanilla-kitchen-cook-stew:
A stew needs two portions of meat, and takes vegetables or eggs as extras. Every slot of the pot you use must hold the same number of portions.

For the Art of Growing firepit, start with dried hay, not freshly cut grass, then finish and light the firepit before cooking. Use vegetables harvested at their edible stage; keep separate plants for seed.
page-vanilla-kitchen-cook-soup:
Pour a portion of water into the pot, then add vegetables, and meat if you have it. Soup stretches a few vegetables a long way.

For the Art of Growing firepit, start with dried hay, not freshly cut grass, then finish and light the firepit before cooking. Vegetables are food-stage harvests, not the final seed-and-rot crop stage.
page-vanilla-kitchen-cook-porridge:
Porridge is two to four portions of grain, with fruit, vegetables or honey as extras. Grain alone barely feeds you; as porridge it fills a bowl.

Dry cereal bundles in sheltered ground piles, thresh the dry pile with a stick, and keep seed bags for planting. Use a knife with spare seeds in the crafting grid to make culinary grain. Use that culinary grain for porridge, not unhulled seed bags. For the Art of Growing firepit, start with dried hay, not freshly cut grass, then finish and light the firepit before cooking.
page-vanilla-preservation-pickle-vegetab:
Put vegetables in a barrel with a litre of brine each, and seal it. They take about two weeks. Pickled vegetables keep far longer than fresh, and curdle milk for cheese.

Harvest vegetables at their edible stage, not the final seed stage. Set aside seed plants, then preserve the food crop with the existing brine recipe.
page-vanilla-stone-age-make-firestarter: Craft a firestarter from two sticks and dried hay, or use Art of Growing’s added straw alternative. Fresh-cut grass must dry before it serves as hay tinder. When lighting a fire, follow the interaction shown for your installed igniter rather than assuming every firestarter works the same way.
page-vanilla-stone-age-knap-shovel:
Knap a shovel head, then put it and a stick in the crafting grid. A shovel digs soil, sand and clay far faster than your hands.

A shovel also helps recover cattail roots. Keep cattail tops as reeds for their own recipes; they are not straw or dried hay.
page-vanilla-stone-age-cut-grass: Cut tall grass with a knife or scythe: Art of Growing leaves a fresh ground layer, not ready dry grass. Let the layer dry in suitable weather, or Sneak-harvest it and dry the fresh grass in a sheltered ground pile. Collect ten dried hay (game:drygrass). Rain and cold can interrupt field drying; fresh grass, hay, straw and aged grass are different materials.
page-vanilla-stone-age-gather-reeds:
Cattails grow in shallow water and on wet shores. Break them, faster with a knife, to get the tops; what's left keeps its root, and grows back.

Use the cattail or papyrus material named by the recipe. Reeds, fresh grass, hay and straw are different materials; do not substitute straw for reeds. Cutting grass instead leaves a fresh layer that must dry for hay.
page-vanilla-stone-age-first-hunt:
Chickens are easy prey. Larger animals fight back: keep your distance until you're better armed.

Fresh grass, straw and named seed bags add trough-feed options, not universal bait. Check the intended animal and trap before using a new crop product as bait.
page-vanilla-stone-age-ground-storage: Sneak + right-click to place supported items on the ground. Art of Growing grass, cereal and flax piles are processing spaces: shelter grass and cereal bundles for drying, thresh dry cereal piles with a stick, and put dry flax stalk piles in water for retting. Ctrl + Sneak + right-click converts a suitably filled hay or straw pile into blocks when the pile offers that action. Tick this only after you have actually stored something. Ground storage guide.
page-vanilla-stone-age-make-fire: Sneak + right-click with dried hay on supported empty ground to start the Art of Growing firepit, then add four firewood and light the completed pit with your igniter’s displayed interaction. Fresh grass is not ready tinder. The ignition goal accepts the firepit family in both the ordinary and Art of Growing domains; it still requires an actual ignition, not just construction.
page-vanilla-stone-age-make-basket:
Ten cattails make a hand basket in the crafting grid. Put it in one of your bag slots for more room to carry.

Use the cattail or papyrus material named by the recipe. Reeds, fresh grass, hay and straw are different materials; do not substitute straw for reeds.
page-vanilla-stone-age-hay-bed: The old eight-hay crafting-grid shortcut is not the Art of Growing route to blocks. Build a hay or straw ground pile and use its Ctrl + Sneak + right-click conversion when sufficiently filled. Three Art of Growing straw blocks (artofgrowing:thatchhay-normal-ud) make its thatch bed. An available ordinary hay bed also counts. Collect the finished bed before placing it to register the obtain goal.
page-vanilla-stone-age-make-torch: Make an unlit torch, then light it at a burning fire. Alongside available ordinary recipes, Art of Growing adds a stick with two straw (game:thatch) for an unlit torch. Freshly cut grass is neither dried hay nor straw. Keep a supply of suitable tinder and torches for night and caves.
page-vanilla-stone-age-cook-roots:
Break a cut cattail again to dig up its root, faster with a shovel. Roast the root on a lit firepit: it's plain, but it keeps you going when nothing else will.

For the Art of Growing firepit, start with dried hay, not freshly cut grass, then finish and light the firepit before cooking.
page-vanilla-stone-age-build-shelter: Raise cob walls and a roof around your bed. Art of Growing adds a soil-and-straw cob route alongside available ordinary recipes; straw is game:thatch from cereal threshing, not fresh-cut grass. Use the displayed cob recipe for quantities. A roof also gives your grass and cereal piles shelter from rain while drying.
page-vanilla-stone-age-make-rope:
Rope is twisted from cattail or papyrus tops, or from wild vines, in the crafting grid. Tongs, ladders and much else need it.

Use the cattail or papyrus material named by the recipe. Reeds, fresh grass, hay and straw are different materials; do not substitute straw for reeds. Rope is also an early route to a rough flax-combing ridge, before you have your first flax twine.
page-vanilla-textiles-grow-flax: Collect sixteen finished flax fibers. Harvest ripe flax as wet cereal bundles, dry them in a sheltered ground pile, then thresh with a stick for seeds and dry flax stalks. Ret the dry stalk pile in water, wash the soaked stalks with water, soften the clean stalks by held right-click, then comb soft stalks with a ridge in your offhand. A rough ridge can use sticks and reed-made rope, so first fibers do not require existing twine. Pick up the finished fibers to register them.
page-vanilla-textiles-spin-twine:
Four flax fibers make a length of flax twine, in the crafting grid. Twine also mends clothing a little.

Flax fibers come after drying and threshing flax bundles, retting the stalks in water, washing, softening and offhand-ridge combing; the crop itself does not give ready fibers. Use four of those finished fibers per twine in the normal crafting-grid recipe.
page-vanilla-wider-world-relight-fire: Rain and snow put out firepits, torches and forges and cool hot metal. Relight a doused fire with a torch, and roof over the ones that matter. See the weather guide. Tick this off once you have. For the Art of Growing firepit, start with dried hay, not freshly cut grass, then finish and light the firepit before cooking. Relighting still needs the extinguished firepit, fuel and an igniter; follow the igniter’s displayed interaction.
page-vanilla-wider-world-make-poultice:
Four horsetail and two cattail or papyrus tops make a poultice. Hold it and right-click to heal your wounds.

Use the cattail or papyrus material named by the recipe. Reeds, fresh grass, hay and straw are different materials; do not substitute straw for reeds. If you choose a flax-fiber recipe, use fully processed, combed fibers rather than raw flax stalks.
page-vanilla-winter-stock-firewood:
Winter is long and cold. Keep plenty of firewood where you can reach it, under a roof.

Stock dried hay or straw separately for tinder and prepare livestock feed before cold weather stops field hay drying. Firewood alone does not cover either need.
page-vanilla-winter-stock-grain: Store sixty-four culinary grain for bread and porridge. First dry and thresh harvested bundles; keep separate planting and appropriate trough-feed seeds before using a knife to hull the surplus. Protect livestock hay and straw reserves too: field hay drying stops in cold conditions, and stored hay and straw eventually age. Do not count raw bundles as ready food grain.
page-vanilla-winter-cellar-food:
Store vegetables in your cellar. Raw vegetables keep best in a storage vessel there.

Harvest vegetables at their edible stage and retain separate seed plants. A cellar food reserve and a dry, checked livestock-feed reserve serve different purposes.
page-vanilla-winter-winter-larder: Gather cured meat and pickles for your own winter larder. Separately check a dry reserve of feed your livestock actually accept, retain planting seeds, and keep straw or dried tinder for fires. Human food goals below do not prove animal winter readiness; complete the feed-reserve check as well. Inspect hay and straw for aging rather than assuming they keep forever.
